Chapter 8: The Collector’s Dilemma—Sacredness, Ownership, and Responsibility.
As collections grow, so do the questions that come with them. What does it really mean to own a sacred image? Is it enough just to admire the artistry and the history, or does owning something sacred come with deeper responsibilities?
For a lot of collectors, these questions don’t show up all at once. Sometimes, it’s a chance encounter or even a sudden spark of self-doubt that brings them to the surface.
Imagine someone who’s spent years gathering Ganesha statues from every corner of the world. One day, she starts to wonder—were some of these pieces taken from places where they truly belonged? Maybe a temple, a family shrine, or a lively village festival? That collection, once a source of pride, now carries a hint of loss—loss for someone else.
Then there’s the collector who visits a museum exhibit on South Asian art. He notices the stark difference between the reverence found in temples and the quiet, almost clinical curiosity of the gallery. He stands in front of a centuries-old Ganesha, picturing the hands that once offered prayers and flowers. Behind the glass, the statue is beautiful, but also feels strangely distant.
These moments of reflection can really shift how people think about collecting. Some decide to return pieces to their original homes or donate them to local organizations. Others turn their attention to supporting artists and craftspeople who are creating new works today, making sure their collections help keep the spirit of Ganesha alive and vibrant.
Of course, there’s rarely an easy answer. The line between appreciation and appropriation can get pretty blurry, and what feels sacred to one person might mean something different to another. But one thing becomes clear—ownership isn’t just about having something. It’s about stewardship, showing respect, and being open to the stories that each piece brings with it.
Through all these challenges, collectors often discover that the real value in their collections isn’t just the objects themselves. It’s about the connections they make—to history, to community, and to those deeper questions that shape every search for meaning.
